images.caption: North Steel, Coquet Island These rocks are covered at high tide and are a danger to shipping. One such wreck was the 'Catherine of Sunderland' which was lost here on 14 Nov 1821. The crew of nine men "clung to the rigging for many hours, imploring assistance from an immense crowd of people who were within reach of their cries, but who were unable to assist them from the absence of a life-boat" [Muray's Handbook:1890].

images.caption: Seals on North Steel Many seals haul out at low tide on the skerries, rocks and Coquet Island itself. There are commercial boats out to the island (but you may not land as it is an RSPB closed reserve) but you can get a lot closer by paddling out in a sea kayak - seals will often come very close to a vessel without an engine to see what you are. Here Mary Waddington paddles a double sea kayak on a Swaledale Outdoor Club trip, while her daughter Sarah takes photographs from the front cockpit - possibly the ideal way to get closeups.

images.caption: Coquet Island Taken from Nether Grange at Alnmouth, five miles away.  It was a monastic site from the 7th century onwards.  The lighthouse was built in 1841, which was manned until 1990 and is now automated.   The island is now an RSPB nature reserve, home to over 30,000 pairs of seabirds.  The public are not allowed to land, although RSPB wardens do stay on the island.
images.alt: Coquet Island Taken from Nether Grange at Alnmouth, five miles away.  It was a monastic site from the 7th century onwards.  The lighthouse was built in 1841, which was manned until 1990 and is now automated.   The island is now an RSPB nature reserve, home to over 30,000 pairs of seabirds.  The public are not allowed to land, although RSPB wardens do stay on the island.
